arc_intro:
FQ-156 — Priya Nair (Cloud Architect)

Good find on that dangling route last time — don't touch it yet, I still want to understand it before we act on it.

Next: I want a full subnet map. FoodQuick's VPC has three subnets, one per AZ, and near as I can tell nobody ever actually decided which of them should be public and which should be private — they're just whatever the default VPC handed us on day one. I need to know exactly what's running where, and what's actually reachable from the internet right now. Start there.

— Priya
arc_outro:
Priya Nair — FQ-156 update:

Good work. foodquick-orders-db is out of the public subnet, the security group is down to a single SG-based rule, and the private route table holds — no path to the internet from there anymore.

One more thing from your report: that 10.50.0.0/16 route pointing to a peering connection that doesn't exist anymore. That's a real thread now, not just noise — something on the other end of that connection USED to talk to this VPC. I want to know what, before we touch it. Keep it flagged. We'll come back to it.

Next up: single points of failure. This whole setup runs like it'll never have a bad day. Let's find out what actually happens when an AZ goes down.

— Priya

tasks.scenario: Before reporting the fix, Priya asks for one line in the incident postmortem doc on what was actually at stake while foodquick-orders-db sat in a public subnet. The DB stores PII and order history for roughly 40,000 daily orders. You pull a comparable case for context: a mid-size Bengaluru fintech had a similarly internet-reachable database found by an automated scanner in 2024, resulting in a customer-data exposure and a ₹9.4 lakh regulatory notice.
tasks.question: FoodQuick's exposure was never actually exploited — the security group happened to still block external access even though the subnet itself was technically public. What's the most accurate way to state this risk in the postmortem?
tasks.solution: The subnet being public did not by itself mean the DB was breached — the security group rule was the only thing standing in the way, and in this case it held. The accurate framing: 'FoodQuick had zero architectural barrier against DB exposure — only a single security group rule stood between the internet and a database holding PII for ~40,000 daily orders. One misconfigured SG change would have made it fully reachable — the same pattern that cost a comparable Bengaluru fintech ₹9.4 lakh in regulatory exposure in 2024.' State the real risk (a missing architectural boundary, a single point of failure), not a false claim that a breach actually happened.

tasks.scenario: You're creating the two new private subnets — subnet-dd44 in ap-south-1a and subnet-ee55 in ap-south-1b. You pick 172.31.0.0/24 for subnet-dd44 without checking what's already allocated in this VPC's 172.31.0.0/16 space.
tasks.error_shown: An error occurred (InvalidSubnet.Conflict) when calling the CreateSubnet operation: The CIDR '172.31.0.0/24' conflicts with another subnet
tasks.diagnosis: A VPC's CIDR block is one shared, finite address pool across every subnet in it. subnet-aa11 already owns 172.31.0.0/20, subnet-bb22 owns 172.31.16.0/20, and subnet-cc33 owns 172.31.32.0/20 — together these consume the entire 172.31.0.0/20 through 172.31.47.255 range. 172.31.0.0/24 falls completely inside subnet-aa11's already-allocated /20 block, so AWS rejects the create — CIDR ranges within one VPC can never overlap, even between subnets that will serve completely different purposes.
tasks.fix: Map out what's already used before picking a new CIDR: 172.31.0.0/20, 172.31.16.0/20, and 172.31.32.0/20 are taken, so the next free /20 blocks start at 172.31.48.0/20. Create subnet-dd44 as 172.31.48.0/20 (ap-south-1a) and subnet-ee55 as 172.31.64.0/20 (ap-south-1b).
